newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: ECNZ defends NZ's new power mkt despite problems.
newsitem.headline: ECNZ defends NZ's new power mkt despite problems.

text.p: Electricity Corporation of New Zealand (ECNZ) on Thursday defended the new wholesale electricity market, despite aberrations in the spot market price which have upset electricity purchasers.

"It's still having its teething problems, it's still bedding down, but we're quite happy with the base market that's been put in place," deputy chief executive Jim Ryniker told journalists at the presentation of ECNZ's annual results.
Ryniker is also a director of the Electricity Market Company (EMCO) which operates the new market.

The aim of the new wholesale market, launched on October 1 this year, is that the price of electricity be determined by the equilibrium between supply and demand. But the market's operation has been hampered by spikes in the spot electricity price, some up to ten times what it used to be.
The Major Electricity Users' Group (MEUG) said unless the aberrations were fixed immediately, consumers would seek government action.
MEUG chairman Terrence Currie said price spikes to more than 50 NZ cents a kilowatt hour had occured on eight of the market's 16 days of operation.
Before the market began, prices had averaged four to five cents per kilowatt hour, but now average prices had on some days reached more than 15 cents, Currie said.

EMCO said some of the spikes were resulting from inconsistencies in data which prevented the computer pricing model from producing prices for some of the 48 half-hour periods it calculated them for. Where these inconsistencies had been identified, procedures had been developed to correct them.

"However, not all of the high prices can be accounted for by data inconsistencies," EMCO said. "There is clearly a mismatch between the information supplied to the market through the price forecast/pre-dispatch scheduling process, and what actually happens in respect of both generation and demand at real time."
ECNZ's Ryniker defended the market's computer pricing model, saying it was more a case of people not having learned how it operated than a problem with the software.

"I don't think there's anything wrong with the models themselves, but not everybody is learning how to work the models properly and people haven't adjusted their behaviours to the market, that's probably its biggest problem."
He said the spikes were occurring at 6 or 7 a.m. as the load came on, "and that load coming on doesn't seem to have been signalled at all through the bidding mechanism by the demandside".

Ryniker said it should not be overlooked that the price spikes were occurring in only one or two of the 48 half-hours and on average, spot prices were probably lower than the hedge prices determined in the day-ahead commitment market.
"But I think the real factor is the market is going to take quite a while to settle down," he said.

In contrast, MEUG's Currie described the new market as a two-wheeled car. "It started I think unproven and untested on the first of October, but already we find that one of the wheels has fallen off," he told Television New Zealand.
